text: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) coordinates environmental responses within the United Nations System and was established in 1972 following the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, with Maurice Strong, its first director, playing a key role in convincing developing nations to prioritize environmental issues. UNEP's mandate includes providing leadership, delivering science, and developing solutions on climate change, marine and terrestrial ecosystem management, and green economic development, while also developing international environmental agreements, publishing environmental science, and supporting national governments in achieving environmental targets. As a member of the United Nations Development Group, UNEP works to help achieve the 17 Sustainable Development Goals. It hosts the secretariats of several multilateral environmental agreements, including the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Minamata Convention on Mercury, the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions, the Convention on Migratory Species, and CITES. In 1988, UNEP and the World Meteorological Organization established the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). UNEP is also an Implementing Agency for the Global Environment Facility and the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol. The agency is sometimes referred to as UN Environment and has its headquarters in Nairobi, Kenya. The location of the headquarters was controversial, with developed countries favoring Geneva and developing countries supporting Nairobi as a symbol of Southern solidarity, despite initial competition from Mexico City, New Delhi, and Cairo. The UN General Assembly elected Maurice Strong as the first head of UNEP in December 1972, and he also served as secretary-general of both the Stockholm Conference and the Earth Summit in 1992. Mostafa Kamal Tolba led UNEP from 1975 to 1992, during which time the Montreal Protocol was negotiated in 1987 to protect the ozone layer. He was succeeded by Elizabeth Dowdeswell (1992–1998), Klaus Töpfer (1998–2006), Achim Steiner (2006–2016), and Erik Solheim (2016–2018). Joyce Msuya became acting executive director in November 2018 after Solheim's resignation and was previously deputy executive director. Inger Andersen was appointed executive director in February 2019 by UN Secretary-General António Guterres. The United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA), established in 2012 to replace the Governing Council, currently has 193 members and meets every two years; its first session was in Nairobi from 23–27 June 2014, the sixth session (UNEA-6) took place in Nairobi from 26 February to 1 March 2024, and the seventh session (UNEA-7) is scheduled for 8–12 December 2025 in Nairobi, with the theme "Advancing sustainable solutions for a resilient planet." UNEP's structure includes eight divisions, and its main activities involve raising awareness on environmental issues. In 1989, UNEP warned that entire nations could be wiped off the Earth by sea level rise if global warming was not reversed by 2000, and in 2005, it predicted that 50 million people could become environmental refugees by 2010, a projection reinforced in 2008 by UN General Assembly President Srgjan Kerim, who estimated between 50 million and 200 million environmental migrants by 2010. At the 2008 Magdeburg Environmental Forum, UNEP and Daimler AG called for infrastructure for electric vehicles under the theme "Sustainable Mobility–the Post-2012 CO2 Agenda." From 1975 to 1995, UNESCO and UNEP led the International Environmental Education Programme, which launched the newsletter Connect in 1976 as a clearinghouse for environmental education information and a network for institutions and individuals until 2007. UNEP is the co-chair and founding partner of the Platform for Accelerating the Circular Economy, a public-private partnership of over 50 global organizations and governments promoting a global circular economy. Established in 1974, the Regional Seas Programme is the world's only legal program for protecting oceans and seas at the regional level, with over 143 countries participating in 18 regional programs under conventions such as the Helsinki, Oslo, Barcelona, and Bucharest Conventions, covering regions including the Caribbean, Mediterranean, Pacific, Arctic, and Black Sea. The Mediterranean Action Plan was established in 1975 as the first regional action plan under this program. In 2017, UNEP launched an initiative to collaborate with faith-based organizations to protect the environment and invest in green resources, publishing in 2020 the book "Faith for Earth: A Call for Action" with the Parliament of the World's Religions Climate Action Program to serve as an educational resource for students, teachers, and leaders. UNEP has established several awards, including the Global 500 Roll of Honour (1987–2003), succeeded in 2005 by Champions of the Earth and Young Champions of the Earth, which annually recognize entrepreneurs, scientists, policy leaders, and individuals for significant environmental contributions. UNEP assigns specific years to environmental topics to raise awareness. The agency has achieved notable successes, such as the 1987 Montreal Protocol to limit ozone-depleting gases and the 2017 Minamata Convention to reduce mercury emissions. UNEP has sponsored solar loan programs to reduce initial costs of solar PV systems, with a notable example being a program that helped 100,000 people finance solar systems in India, leading to similar projects in Tunisia, Morocco, Indonesia, and Mexico. In 2001, UNEP released satellite images showing that 90 percent of the Iraqi marshlands had been lost, and began supporting the environmental management of the marshlands in 2004. UNEP has a youth program called Tunza, including the AEO for Youth project. In 2007, following the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report, the Paris Call for Action, supported by 46 countries including EU nations but excluding the United States, Saudi Arabia, Russia, and China, called for replacing UNEP with a stronger "United Nations Environment Organization" modeled on the World Health Organization. In December 2012, after the Rio+20 Summit, the UN General Assembly decided to strengthen and upgrade UNEP and establish universal membership in its governing body, transitioning from a system of 58 executive member states to universal membership of all UN member states, implemented in 2014. In 2015, the European Investment Bank and UNEP created the Renewable Energy Performance Platform (REPP) with $67 million from the UK's International Climate Finance initiative and $128 million in 2018, aiming to improve energy access for at least two million people in Sub-Saharan Africa over five years, having invested around $45 million in renewable energy projects across 13 countries, using solar and hydropower. In September 2018, allegations were made against UNEP executive director Erik Solheim regarding excessive time spent outside Nairobi, leading to his resignation; several donor countries, including the Netherlands, Sweden, and Denmark, withdrew funding, with the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs stating the fund freezing was unprecedented.
